title: Architecture standards: API / coding / infra / model-serving / observability / performance (Unified)
author: Ava Martinez
content:
Purpose and scope

This page consolidates Redwood Inference's architecture and engineering standards across API design, coding practices, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, and performance. It is intended as the canonical reference for architects, service owners, and onboarding engineers. The document includes normative rules, rationale, ownership, and example ADRs for recent cross-cutting decisions.

Audience
- Engineering teams (service owners, backend, infra, ML infra)
- Platform and SRE teams
- Product and security reviewers

High-level principles (applies to all sections)
- Predictability first: performance and cost budgets must be explicit for any externally facing service.
- Developer ergonomics: standards should enable fast, safe iteration.
- Observability by default: every service must produce metrics, traces, and structured logs at the minimum levels specified below.
- Backwards compatibility: public APIs and SDKs require versioned rollout and deprecation timelines.

1) API standards (owner: API Platform)
Goal: consistent, stable, and discoverable HTTP/REST and RPC interfaces for hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
Norms:
- Use OpenAPI v3 for all HTTP services and publish the spec to api-redwood (internal registry) before first release.
- Use RESTful resource modeling for read/write operations and HTTP/2 or gRPC for high-throughput internal RPCs.
- Standard response envelope: {"status":<string>,"data":<object|null>,"error":<object|null>} (JSON).
- Pagination: cursor-based (stable opaque token).
- Rate limiting: per-customer token bucket; include headers X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset.
- Versioning: major in path (/v1/...), minor changes via feature flags and content-negotiation headers.
- Authentication: all public API calls must use token-based auth (Bearer + scoped API keys). Private deployments may integrate via mutual TLS (mTLS) per customer config.

Required artifacts before launch:
- OpenAPI spec (api-redwood registry link)
- Example SDK snippets (python, js)
- Backwards compatibility checklist and deprecation plan

2) Coding standards (owner: Eng DX)
Purpose: Maintainable, reviewable, and secure code across polyglot services.
Key rules:
- Language-specific style guides are normative: Python (PEP8 + Black), Go (gofmt + go vet), TypeScript (eslint + prettier).
- Mandatory static analysis: SAST for backend code (Bandit/semgrep ruleset), typed builds for TypeScript, and unit-test coverage minimum 60% for critical paths.
- PR requirements: description with design, test plan, telemetry changes, and at least one reviewer from service team + one from platform for infra-impacting changes.
- Secrets: do not commit secrets. Use HashiCorp Vault or cloud KMS integrations.
- Dependency management: monthly automated dependency update PRs; high/critical CVE must be remediated within 48 hours of detection.

3) Infrastructure standards (owner: Eng Infra)
Goal: scalable, cost-efficient, and secure infra across hosted, dedicated, and private offerings.
Standards:
- IaC: Terraform (>=1.3) modules for cloud resources; modules live in terraform-modules repo with peer-reviewed changes.
- Environments: clear separation: dev, staging, prod; use identical IaC templates with config parameters.
- Network: zero-trust default - internal services use service-to-service mTLS; customer-facing private deployments must support customer-managed VPC peering and explicit firewall rules.
- Secrets & keys: KMS for key wrapping; HSM available for Private customers per contract.
- Provisioning policy: GPU fleet autoscaling policies defined in fleet-config.yml (example table below).

GPU fleet autoscale policy (example)
| pool_name | min_nodes | max_nodes | scale_up_threshold (p90) | scale_down_idle_minutes |
| inference-pool-a | 4 | 200 | 85% utilization | 15 |
| batch-pool-b | 2 | 50 | queued_jobs > 30 | 30 |

4) Model-serving standards (owner: Serving Runtime)
Objective: predictable latency, cost, and correctness for model inference across variants and hardware.
Mandatory controls:
- Model manifests: every model must include a manifest.json with schema_version, architecture, tokenizer, quantization_profile, validated_input_schema, and observed_perf_profiles (p50/p95/p99 latency, memory, tokens/s).
- Quantization profiles: label supported quantization modes for each hardware target and include accuracy/regression test results.
- KV cache semantics: explicit contract for ephemeral cache invalidation and customer-visible cache-control headers for responses that can be cached.
- Routing policy: requests must be routable by policy (latency-first, cost-first, region-bound). Default policy = latency-first for premium tier, cost-first for free tier.
- Canary & rollback: model rollouts must use canary traffic (5% -> 20% -> 100%) with automated metric gates (error rate, regen quality score) and an automated rollback window of 30 minutes on regressions.

Model manifest sample (text representation)
- model_id: redwood/gptx-8k-v1
- schema_version: 1.2
- architectures: transformer-blocks: 64, hidden: 8192
- quant_profiles: a2fp16, int8-qat
- perf_profiles: {hosted-gpu-a100: p50=45ms, p95=210ms}

5) Observability standards (owner: Eng Platform + SRE)
Intent: fast MTTI/MTTR and continuous quality measurement.
Minimum telemetry for any service:
- Metrics (Prometheus): request_total (labels: route, method, status), latency_seconds_bucket (histogram), error_rate, tokens_generated_total (for inference services), cache_hit_ratio.
- Tracing (OpenTelemetry): trace for 100% of errors and 1% of successful requests sampled for latency distribution; include trace context propagation across internal RPCs.
- Logs (structured JSON): include request_id, customer_id, route, model_id, and error_code. Write logs to centralized ELK/Opensearch with 30-day retention default.
- Alerting: SLO-based alerts only - no pager for symptom without SLO breach.

SLO table (examples)
| service_type | availability | latency_p95 | error_budget | paging_policy |
| hosted-api | 99.95% monthly | gen p95 < 350ms | 0.05% | page on sustained breach > 30m |
| dedicated-gateway | 99.9% monthly | p95 < 500ms | 0.1% | page on immediate breach |

6) Performance standards and benchmarking (owner: Eng Serving Runtime + Perf)
Goals: predictable token cost and tail latency across common workloads.
- Benchmarks: maintain benchmark suites for gen, chat, and embedding workloads. Benchmarks must include: sequence length distributions, batch sizes, KV cache warm vs cold, and mixed-request patterns.
- Baseline targets: for a 4k sequence on A100-like hardware, median per-token latency <10ms and p95 token latency <40ms for optimized models. These targets are model-dependent and must be documented in model perf_profiles.
- Regression testing: every model or runtime change must run the perf-suite; regressions >5% in p95 or cost must block rolling to prod until owner-approved mitigation is in place.

7) Decision records (ADRs) - canonical examples
ADR 2025-12-02: Unified API Envelope (Author: Noah Green)
- Problem: Inconsistent error payloads across services caused downstream SDK complexity.
- Decision: Adopt a standard API response envelope with keys status/data/error and map all existing services to the envelope over a two-quarter migration window.
- Alternatives considered: keep per-service error shapes (rejected), adopt HTTP problem+json (rejected as insufficient for telemetry needs).
- Consequences: SDKs simplified; migration requires compatibility layer for two quarters.

ADR 2026-01-18: Default Routing Policy for Hosted Customers (Author: Priya Rao)
- Problem: Customers saw large performance variance when runtime selected cheaper model variants by default.
- Decision: Make default policy latency-first for paid tiers and cost-first for free/low-tier. Customers can override through route config.
- Monitoring: Add autopolicy metric to track percent of requests served cost-first vs latency-first.

Operational runbook summary (links and steps)
- Runbook: Model rollout failure (link: confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/model-rollout-failure)
  1. Pause rollout via control-plane UI or cli: redwoodctl rollout pause <model_id>
  2. Re-route traffic to previous stable manifest: redwoodctl route set --manifest <stable_manifest>
  3. Notify SRE and owning team, start postmortem if >30m outage

Ownership and governance
- Owners listed above are accountable for the standards and must review exceptions.
- Exceptions: documented via Exception Request (templates/exceptions) and require at least two reviewers (owner + SRE).
- Review cadence: quarterly review of standards with public changelog and ADR archive.

Onboarding checklist for new services
1. Create OpenAPI spec and register in api-redwood.
2. Add Terraform module and create dev/staging/prod pipelines.
3. Add Prometheus metrics and OpenTelemetry tracing hooks.
4. Add model manifest (if applicable) and perf-profile placeholder.
5. Run unit and perf tests; attach results to PR.

References and links
- api-redwood registry (internal)
- terraform-modules repo (internal)
- model-manifest-spec (confluence/eng-serving-runtime/model-manifest-spec-2025-10-01)
- ADR index (confluence/architecture-and-standards/adr-index)

Appendix: common checklist snippet (can be pasted into PR template)
- [ ] OpenAPI spec included and published
- [ ] Unit tests (>=60% coverage on critical paths)
- [ ] Perf suite run for runtime-impacting changes
- [ ] Prometheus metrics and traces instrumented
- [ ] Secrets and keys stored in Vault
- [ ] Owners and oncall assigned

If you need an exception or help mapping these standards to a specific service, contact the standards owners (eng-architecture@redwood.com) or open a standards review ticket.
